content.title: Vaccines
content.text: Vaccines train your immune system to recognize and respond to certain diseases, so your body is best equipped to fight back. Many vaccines prevent disease or serious illness, helping to protect your health. Vaccines are one of the most important tools we have for protecting against serious and sometimes deadly infectious diseases.Vaccines teach your body to recognize and fight pathogens and other foreign substances like viruses and bacteria - so your immune system is ready if you encounter them in the future. Vaccines do this by using a harmless component of the pathogen—such as a weakened or inactivated form of a virus—allowing your body to build protection without causing illnessThere are several types of vaccines, and while they can differ in design, every vaccine is developed with one goal: to protect you and your loved ones from serious illness. Some vaccines provide long-lasting protection against pathogens that don’t change much overtime, like polio, measles, and hepatitis B. Others, like the flu shot, target viruses that change frequently, so the vaccine needs updating to match circulating strains. There are also therapeutic vaccines, which are being studied to help the body fight diseases a person already has, such as certain cancers.Vaccines are important because they protect people from serious and potentially life-threatening diseases. They train the body’s immune system to fight germs before they cause disease, keeping individuals and families safer. And they play a critical role in improving public health by preventing and largely removing dangerous diseases like polio and smallpox, saving millions of lives and preventing countless hospitalizations. Vaccines are very safe, and they are the best way to protect yourself and your family from serious illness. Millions of children receive vaccines safely every year. While all medical products may have the risk of side effects, the most common side effects of vaccines are very mild and short, such as pain or swelling at the injection site. The United States has an extremely thorough and layered vaccine safety system. Before a vaccine is approved by the FDA, it must go through years of testing and a robust clinical trial process to show that its benefits outweigh the potential risks. Even after approval, vaccines are closely monitored for safety.It’s completely understandable that a parent of a child with autism would want answers about the cause of the disorder. Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition with a strong genetic component. The question about vaccines and autism has been asked and thoroughly answered. Instead of continuing down this path we should be putting resources and energy into promising research that can help us better understand real factors that contribute to this complex condition.High vaccination rates are critical to preventing outbreaks of serious diseases and keeping people healthy. When large percentages of people are vaccinated, it creates a strong shield of protection that helps stop infections from spreading.Even though other people may be vaccinated, diseases can still spread if too many people skip their shots. By getting vaccinated – you’re protecting yourself and protecting vulnerable people from the disease reaching them. When more people are vaccinated, everyone stays safer.Vaccines are made up of different ingredients. Antigens are the active ingredient in a vaccine. Some ingredients help boost the immune response of a vaccine, while others ensure the vaccine works safely and provides long-lasting protection against disease. Every ingredient in a vaccine is extensively reviewed and tested for safety.Not all vaccines work the same, but they all serve a common purpose: to protect against infections. Some vaccines prevent individuals from contracting a specific disease. These vaccines are effective against viruses and bacteria that change very little over time, such polio, measles, and hepatitis B. Since they can provide long-lasting protection, they are not needed on a recurring schedule. Other vaccines protect you against severe disease and are used against viruses and bacteria that undergo frequent changes. Think about the seasonal flu vaccine – it is updated every year to help your immune system respond to the latest changes to the virus.Hepatitis B is a serious liver infection, and babies are particularly vulnerable. Infants infected at birth have a 90% chance of developing chronic infection, which can lead to cirrhosis, liver cancer or liver failure. Hepatitis B is up to 100 times more infectious than HIV and the virus can live outside the body for up to a week. It can be passed to infants by an infected mother, family member or caregiver during pregnancy or birth, through cuts or bites or even by sharing personal items with someone who is infected. That’s why giving the vaccine at birth is so important – it protects newborns immediately, when they need it most and before they can be exposed. The benefits of the vaccine outweigh the risks, and the vaccine is 95-99% effective in preventing hepatitis B infection and the associated long-term complications.When vaccines are delayed, children stay unprotected longer when they are most vulnerable. Some vaccines are combination vaccines that have been around for decades. These vaccines help limit the number of trips to the doctor’s office and lead to fewer shots. Today’s recommended vaccine schedule is carefully developed to ensure children are protected at the ages when they’re most likely to face serious illness. The schedule is based on decades of research to make sure kids get protection exactly when they’re needed most.It is important to have access to vaccines so that every American has the ability to protect themselves and their families from disease. Ensuring that Americans can get vaccines with no out-of-pocket costs allows people to make the best choice for their family without financial barriers.
